Since I presented essentially that argument yesterday here, I'm going to address this.

Though I'll note, first, that that's not really the argument I presented, since I said nothing about people starting their own subs. I wrote about treating Voat as a free market, in which each and all are free to offer up whatever subs they might want, including with whatever rules they might want, and consumers are free to direct their business to whatever subs offer whatever it is that best corresponds with their preferences.

and people should be able to govern how they like on their own subs.

Yes - this is my view, and here's why.

Subs will be governed, no matter what. That is to say, there will be some mechanism(s) in place - formal or informal - by which some set of norms will be to some degree enforced. That is simply unavoidable - it's the nature of any purposeful collective. A sub exists in order to provide a place for communication of some particular form - between a particular group of people and/or centered on a particular topic and/or in a particular style, etc. That means that a sub is purposeful, which means that there will be some mechanism(s) in place to maintain it. That can range anywhere from the equivalent of a dictatorship to the equivalent of a democracy, but the fact remains that there will be some "government," no matter what.

There's an enormous range of preferences there - there are users who want the closest thing to anarchy they can get, and there are users who want the security of a dictatorship in which all are forced to march in lockstep around a single topic, and all things in between. Therefore, I believe that the interests of all the users of this site are best served by allowing anyone who is so minded to provide any sort of sub they might prefer, with any ruleset they might prefer. That way, all of the users of this site have the maximum opportunity to find whatever it is that they're looking for here, since individual subs are allowed to shape themselves however they please, and appeal to whoever they might prefer to appeal to. If they take a form that is pleasing to enough people, they will be rewarded with "customers." If they don't, then they won't. I see no need for any mechanism beyond that, and in fact consider any mechanism beyond that to be a direct threat to the liberty that each and all of the users here should have to seek out whatever forums and whatever rules they might prefer.

And yes - that does run into a problem with the "default" subs, since that mechanism - the popularity of the sub being an expression of the approval or lack thereof of the ruleset - is undermined by the sub's default status.

Honestly, I'm not sure how to deal with that. My comments here and elsewhere on the topic spring from the fact that I am sure that the empowerment of one group of individuals to decree what is or is not acceptable on other subs is NOT the best way to do so. That simply establishes an even greater authority than that which any individuals might hold over individual subs, and thus a greater threat capable of greater abuse, and with site-wide effects, rather than effects limited to individual subs.

It seems that the issue breaks over the notion of "default" subs. I'm sure there are some who want the authority to decree what is or is not acceptable on any and all subs, but at least the cooler heads have pulled back to a stated position that it's somehow necessary to exercise that kind of authority over at least default subs, simply because they're defaults.

It seems to me then that the better approach is to at least redefine what it means to be a "default" sub, and possibly do away with the whole concept.

It might work better if the "default" subs were just the current trending subs in any of a range of broad categories. So if a sub is currently popular, it will end up as the one first shown to new visitors when they look for something in that particular category. And if it takes a direction that's unpopular with the community, its rating will fall (key it to increase/decrease in views rather than overall subscribers, for instance) and something else will become the "default." That could settle the problem without the worrying precedent of giving some few effective authority over what should or should not be allowed site-wide. So, for instance, with a system like that, askgoat would've replaced askvoat as the "default" question sub weeks ago, and without any need for any authoritarian action. And that way, it's at least more likely that the "default" subs will end up being the ones that actually are the most attractive to the community.
